strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use an elitist, real-valued differential-evolution search on the capped simplex, followed by a short derivative-free poll along dense, mass-preserving directions. Score every feasible candidate with the exact finite-lag objective. This is materially different from the supplied LP trust-region search and the previous smooth-max SLSQP and two-coordinate exchange approaches: it uses neither a lag linearization, a smoothed objective, gradients, nor pairwise-only moves. Population mutation and crossover make coordinated changes to many samples and explore multiple basins; the final poll makes bounded multi-coordinate refinements around the best candidate.

Use the supplied initial_h_values directly as the first candidate and, if feasible, preserve it as an untouched fallback. The exact objective and joint feasibility projection are mathematical requirements; the choice of evolutionary search, its mutation rules, and the claim that they may explore useful basins are heuristics. The objective is nonconvex, and a finite evolutionary search and poll have no global-optimality guarantee and may fail to improve the parent. Do not claim an improvement or a measured score.

2. Mathematical specification
For the runtime resolution n, let dx = 2/n and s = n/2. A candidate is h in R^n and must satisfy 0 <= h[i] <= 1 and sum_i h[i] = s, so dx times its sum is 1. For every integer lag d from -(n-1) through n-1, define a=max(d,0), b=max(-d,0), and m=n-|d|. Define

Q_d(h) = dx * sum over r=0,...,m-1 of h[a+r] * (1-h[b+r]), and C(h) = max_d Q_d(h).

This is the same set of 2n-1 lag values as np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full') * dx. Each lag uses only its finite overlap of n-|d| terms; indices do not wrap around. Include both lag directions. The program must use the exact correlation expression for scoring, not a circular correlation or a boundary-free autocorrelation identity. The products make the objective nonconvex; no convexity or global-optimum assumption is used.

For any finite vector z, the joint Euclidean projection onto the feasible set has coordinates

Pi(z)[i] = clip(z[i]-lambda, 0, 1),

where lambda is chosen so that sum_i Pi(z)[i]=s. The sum is continuous and nonincreasing in lambda, so bisection finds it; a capacity-limited residual correction handles floating-point error. This projection enforces the box and mass conditions jointly.

For population members x_i, differential evolution uses either rand/1 mutation
m_i = x_r1 + F_i * (x_r2-x_r3),
or current-to-best/1 mutation
m_i = x_i + F_i * (x_best-x_i) + F_i * (x_r2-x_r3),
with distinct random population indices other than i. Every member has sum s, so these mutations preserve the sum algebraically, but can violate box bounds. Binomial crossover selects mutant or target coordinates and generally changes the sum, so project the crossed vector with Pi before scoring. All selection is by exact C(h); there is no surrogate.

For the final poll, a direction v has sum zero. A trial h+t*v preserves mass. Its exact feasible interval is the intersection of coordinate bounds: for v[i]>0, t is in [-h[i]/v[i], (1-h[i])/v[i]]; for v[i]<0, t is in [(1-h[i])/v[i], -h[i]/v[i]]; a zero coordinate imposes no restriction. The poll tests specified positive and negative step lengths inside this interval, projects only to remove roundoff, and ranks trials by exact C.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Write one top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs) and top-level helper functions only. Use NumPy and the standard library; no solver is required. Do not use closures or lambdas. Keep input checks, projection, random search, exact scoring, recovery, and output construction in the generated program. Read initial_h_values only as the optional runtime global supplied by the harness; do not redefine, serialize, reconstruct, or hard-code its entries.

3.2. Resolve the resolution before constructing candidates. Try to convert initial_h_values to a flattened float64 array. If its length is in [1,999], set n to that length and retain that resolution even if its values are later rejected. If no valid parent length exists, accept kwargs['n_points'] only when it converts to an integer in [1,999]; otherwise set n=47. Ignore a requested resolution when a valid parent length is available. Thus this plan does not transfer a parent between resolutions.

A parent is usable if its entries are finite and lie in [-1e-8, 1+1e-8]. If it is already within [0,1] and its mass residual is within the feasibility tolerance, preserve a float64 copy as the parent fallback and first search candidate. Otherwise clip only tolerated tiny excursions and pass the parent through the joint projection. If the parent is absent or unusable, use the uniform vector full(n, 0.5). If parent projection fails, also use the uniform vector. Keep this fallback in a separate array that search operations never mutate. Convert seed to int for one NumPy default_rng; if conversion fails, use 42. Ignore unrelated kwargs.

3.3. Implement project_capped(z,n), is_feasible(h,n), and exact_score(h,n) as top-level helpers. project_capped rejects a wrong shape or nonfinite input and clips finite working values to [-1e12,1e12]. Bisect lambda for 80 iterations on [min(z)-1, max(z)]: the lower endpoint gives a clipped sum of n, and the upper gives zero. If the sum at the midpoint exceeds s, move the lower endpoint up; otherwise move the upper endpoint down. Form clip(z-lambda,0,1) at the final midpoint. Correct the residual s-sum(h) by visiting coordinates in ascending order and adding no more than 1-h[i] for a positive residual, or subtracting no more than h[i] for a negative residual. Recompute the residual after each change and stop when its magnitude is at most 1e-12 or a full pass has no capacity. Return failure if the residual exceeds 1e-10*max(1,n), or any output is nonfinite or outside [0,1]. Do not replace this with clipping followed by rescaling.

is_feasible requires shape (n,), finite entries, bounds within a 1e-12 numerical check, and mass residual at most 1e-10*max(1,n). Constructed and returned candidates must in fact be inside [0,1]; reproject candidates before final acceptance if needed. exact_score returns positive infinity for an infeasible candidate or nonfinite correlation. Otherwise it computes float(max(np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode='full') * (2.0/n))). This is the authoritative score and includes every finite-support lag.

3.4. Construct an initial pool algorithmically. Pass every proposed vector through project_capped before adding it. In order, propose the fallback, its reversal, 1-fallback, 1-fallback[::-1], the uniform vector, a block with floor(n/2) leading ones and, when n is odd, a following 0.5, an alternating zero/one vector, a seeded balanced binary vector, two seeded fallback-plus-Gaussian-noise vectors with standard deviations 0.08 and 0.22, two seeded uniform random vectors, and two circular shifts of the fallback by floor(n/3) and floor(n/2). A balanced binary vector is made by a seeded permutation: place floor(n/2) ones at the first permuted positions; if n is odd place 0.5 at the next position; leave the others zero. All starts, including transformations that appear feasible algebraically, go through the projection.

Deduplicate starts when their maximum coordinate difference is below 1e-8. Score every retained start with exact_score and initialize the global best to the better of the fallback and the starts. Keep the fallback separate even if it is also in the pool. If there are more distinct starts than the population size, keep the fallback and global best, then add the remaining starts in ascending exact-score order. Fill the population to its specified size using a seeded mixture: 45% projected Gaussian perturbations of the current best, 25% perturbations of randomly chosen existing members, 15% projected uniform vectors, and 15% balanced binary vectors. For Gaussian perturbations, choose sigma from {0.03, 0.08, 0.16, 0.32} and multiply it by scale_n=clip(sqrt(47/n),0.5,1.5). Try at most 6*population_size additions to obtain distinct members; if necessary, fill remaining slots with copies of the best feasible member. Score all population members exactly. For n=1, skip evolution and polling and return the feasible uniform vector.

3.5. Run synchronous differential evolution: every trial in one generation is made from the population snapshot at the start of that generation. For each target, choose F from its stored value, initially sampled uniformly from [0.45,0.85], and CR initially from [0.4,0.9]. With probability 0.1 replace the trial F by 0.35+0.55*U; with probability 0.1 replace trial CR by 0.10+0.85*U, where U is a seeded uniform draw. Choose rand/1 or current-to-best/1 with probability 0.5 each. Select the required distinct indices uniformly without replacement from indices other than the target. Use the best member of the current snapshot as x_best.

For each coordinate, copy from the mutant with probability CR and otherwise copy from the target. Force one uniformly selected coordinate to come from the mutant. Project the crossed vector, reject it if projection fails, and compute its exact score. Replace the target only when the trial score is less than its score by more than 1e-12. On acceptance, retain the trial F and CR for that member; on rejection, retain the old parameters. Update the global best whenever any feasible trial improves its exact score by more than 1e-12. After forming the next population, ensure a copy of global_best is present: if not, replace the worst-scoring member and store global_score there. Never discard a better global candidate because of population replacement or a tie.

3.6. Count generations without a global improvement greater than 1e-12. At the size-dependent stall limit in section 4, restart only if the allotted restart count has not been used. Sort the current population by exact score; retain its best quarter, with at least two members, and ensure global_best is among them. Fill the other slots by projecting and scoring candidates: half are Gaussian perturbations of global_best, one quarter are perturbations of randomly selected retained members, and one quarter are fresh projected uniform or balanced binary vectors, chosen equally often. For restart number r starting at zero, use Gaussian sigma 0.06, 0.16, or 0.32 according to r, multiplied by scale_n and capped at 0.45. Initialize F and CR for new members from their original ranges. Reset the stall counter and continue within the fixed generation limit. Preserve the fallback throughout. If the restart allowance is exhausted, continue the remaining generations without another restart.

3.7. After evolution, perform a derivative-free multi-coordinate pattern poll from global_best. Begin with delta=0.12*scale_n, capped at 0.25. In each round generate the configured number of directions. Half are seeded standard-normal vectors with their mean subtracted; the rest are differences of two distinct members from the best quarter of the current population, with global_best included if needed. Subtract each direction's mean, divide it by its maximum absolute coordinate, and skip it if that maximum is zero or nonfinite. Compute its feasible interval from the coordinate formulas in section 2. If the interval is invalid, skip the direction.

For each direction, test t values obtained by clipping -delta, -delta/2, delta/2, and delta to the feasible interval. Skip values with magnitude at most 1e-12 and duplicate values within 1e-12. Form h+t*v, pass it through project_capped to remove floating-point mass error, validate it, and calculate exact_score. At the end of a round, accept the best trial only if it improves global_score by more than 1e-12. If a round improves the score, set delta=min(0.25,1.2*delta); otherwise halve delta. Stop at the configured round limit or when delta<1e-4. The poll is a finite set of exact-objective evaluations, not a surrogate line minimization.

3.8. Finalize inside run. Reproject global_best, validate it, and recompute its exact score. If this fails, use the separately stored fallback. Use a searched candidate only if its recomputed score is lower than fallback_score by more than 1e-12; otherwise select the fallback. Validate and score the selected vector again. If any exception, invalid state, or failed recovery remains, use full(n,0.5), which is feasible for every supported n, and compute its exact score. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a float64 NumPy array of length n, c5_bound a Python float recomputed by exact_score, and n_points an integer.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use these defaults without preliminary experiments. For n in [1,64], use population size 40, at most 120 generations, stall limit 20, at most 3 restarts, 28 poll rounds, and 10 directions per round. For n in [65,128], use 36, 90, 16, 2, 20, and 8 respectively. For n in [129,256], use 28, 55, 12, 1, 12, and 6. For n in [257,512], use 20, 30, 10, 1, 8, and 4. For n in [513,999], use 14, 18, 8, 1, 5, and 4. The n=1 case bypasses search. Population sizes are at least 8 wherever evolution is run.

The fixed defaults for projection are 80 bisection iterations and the tolerances in section 3. The default mutation-strategy mixture is equal rand/1 and current-to-best/1; F, CR, crossover, and restart rules are as specified above. Practical variations within this same approach are population sizes of 32-48 for n<=64, strategy probabilities between 0.35 and 0.65, and modest changes to generation or poll counts while decreasing them as n grows. Poll rounds may use 4-12 directions and step sizes between 0.08 and 0.18 initially. Use the specified defaults when no runtime budget setting is supplied. Any score-dependent restart, step-size change, or population selection must be an operation inside the generated program. The full lag formula, joint feasibility, exact-score comparison, and fallback preservation are correctness requirements, not tunable choices.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 arrays and the seeded generator for every random choice. The population requires O(M*n) storage, where M is at most 40 and n at most 999. Each exact score uses np.correlate and O(n) output memory with O(n^2) arithmetic. Do not allocate a dense lag-by-coordinate gradient, Hessian, or pair-by-lag matrix. The restart and generation counts decrease with n, and execution is single-process on one CPU.

Projection must reject nonfinite inputs, bound its bisection interval using the clipped finite vector, and correct mass only within available coordinate capacity. Check all trial vectors and all scores for finiteness. If mutation arithmetic, projection, or scoring fails for one trial, skip that trial and retain the existing feasible member. Catch exceptions around a search stage so they do not erase the best candidate or fallback. Keep exact-score comparisons monotone for accepted DE replacements and for the final poll. Terminate by the explicit generation, restart, poll-round, and delta limits; no convergence or global-optimality guarantee is claimed. If search produces no improvement, return the validated fallback rather than an unvalidated proposal.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must define run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and return the required three-tuple. It must derive dimensions from the runtime parent or the permitted n_points fallback, keep n in [1,999], and use the supplied initial_h_values without embedding or reconstructing it. Before scoring or accepting any candidate, check its shape, finiteness, bounds, and mass; project search proposals jointly onto the capped simplex. Implement the exact full linear-correlation score in program code and use it for starts, every evolutionary trial, every poll trial, fallback comparison, and the returned score. Never select by a mutation heuristic or approximate score alone.

Retain a feasible parent-derived fallback whenever a usable parent is supplied and retain the uniform fallback for recovery. Keep the fallback separate from all mutable population arrays. Before returning, validate the selected vector and recompute C(h) from the exact evaluator formula. On invalid candidates or unexpected failures, recover to the parent-derived fallback when valid, otherwise to full(n,0.5). Return no filesystem or network output; return only the specified vector, its recomputed exact bound, and its integer resolution.
